extracted.intended_audience: writers/producers of late-night satirical TV (Daily Show / Last Week Tonight) and comedy writers crafting news-parody segments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and writing satirical television segments in the style of The Daily Show and Last Week Tonight, covering format elements, comedic voice, production tools, and a five-question evaluation rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Monologue
rubrics_metrics.description: Opening Monologue — summary of day's main stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the three major elements of The Daily Show format; typically a concise roundup that frames the night's satire. Uses news conventions (clips, soundbites) and benefits from rapid iterative drafting under tight schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mockumentary Feature (correspondent field report)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mockumentary Feature — correspondent does fake field report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recurring element where a correspondent performs a faux on-the-scene report; exploits the correspondent 'in over their head' persona and uses reporter-package conventions for comedic contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview Segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview Segment — celebrity or political figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A traditional interview slot adapted for comedy; can be used to juxtapose serious content with comedic framing or to draw out absurdities from guests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of News Conventions Adapted for Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: News conventions (video clips, soundbites, reporter packages, news graphics, anchor-correspondent banter) are repurposed as comedic material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements should be treated as raw material for satire—e.g., juxtapose clips or exaggerate graphics for comedic effect; blending real news form with absurd content is a core technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative Writing Process and Tempo
rubrics_metrics.description: Insane daily schedule; 4–5 drafts of each script; segments put together in as little as 24 hours; longer pieces: up to a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rapid cycles of rewriting for topical pieces; longer investigative or in-depth segments permit more development time. Process discipline (multiple drafts) is part of producing polished satire under deadline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan Delivery / Disbelief-Based Comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadpan delivery of absurd content; frame with deadpan disbelief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present absurdities in a straight-faced manner to heighten contrast. The voice should convey sincere incredulity rather than obvious silliness; this anchors the satire and makes the absurd reveal land harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of Clips to Reveal Contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Juxtaposition of clips (showing politicians contradicting themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use side-by-side or successive clips to expose hypocrisy, inconsistency, or absurdity. This editing technique is a primary mechanism for turning source material into satirical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor Reaction Shots
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor reaction shots as a comedic device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anchor expressions and timing to signal audience response or disbelief; reaction shots can punctuate a joke or highlight the absurdity of the presented material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondent-in-Over-Their-Head Persona
rubrics_metrics.description: Correspondent in over their head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray correspondents as earnest but outmatched by the situation to generate sympathy and laughter; this persona helps carry mockumentary pieces and contrasts with anchor deadpan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Last Week Tonight: Few Short Segments Plus One In-Depth Main Segment
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure — Few short segments related to recent news + ONE main segment in depth (15–25 minutes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The show typically uses brief topical items to warm up before an extended, researched main segment that explores a single topic at length. The main segment's length (15–25 minutes) allows cumulative argument and sustained satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main Segment May Cover Non-Current Topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Main segment can cover topics not in current news cycle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer-form treatment permits choosing systemic or evergreen topics that benefit from deep explanation; not every main segment needs to be strictly 'breaking news.'

rubrics_metrics.name: In-Depth Treatment Builds Cumulative Absurdity and Educates
rubrics_metrics.description: More time = more thorough satire; can build cumulative absurdity; educational + entertainment hybrid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the extended runtime to layer information and jokes so that each beat amplifies the previous, leading to an escalating comedic and rhetorical payoff while informing the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Varied Comedy Tools (animation, stunts, fake commercials, stingers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy Tools — animation breaks; stunts (purchasing things, sponsorship parodies); fake commercials; final '...and now this' type segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix formats and media (animation, live stunts, parody ads) to vary pace and introduce surprise; these tools can illustrate points or provide transitional beats in a long segment.

rubrics_metrics.name: John Oliver's Voice Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: John Oliver's Voice — high moral indignation; British rage at absurdity; surreal tangents; calls to action ('Go to thiswebsite.com').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voice combines righteous anger with comedic digression and clear calls-to-action; maintaining a consistent persona (moralist-but-humorous) helps unify long-form segments and motivates the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Source Video as Material
rubrics_metrics.description: Source video as material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat broadcast footage, clips, and soundbites as primary inputs for discoveries of contradiction or absurdity that can be mined and recontextualized for jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find the Contradiction or Absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the contradiction or absurdity in source material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify moments where claims, actions, or formats reveal hypocrisy, illogic, or unintended comedy; this discovery is the seed for the segment's argument and jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build to a Compound or Escalating Reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: Build to compound joke at the end / Does the segment build to an escalating reveal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure material so that each beat raises stakes or adds information, culminating in a revealing payoff that re-frames earlier content for maximal comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear Point of View (Not Neutral)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it have a clear point of view (not just neutral)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective satire takes an explicit stance—moral, political, or rhetorical—rather than feigning neutrality. A clear POV helps tie together evidence and comedic argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real News Premise
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a real news premise?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segments should be grounded in an actual newsworthy situation or verifiable factual premise; this anchors satire in reality and increases its persuasive and comedic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy Must Be Deadpan / Disbelief-Based (explicit rubric item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the comedy deadpan / disbelief-based?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The explicit rubric emphasizes a straight delivery of absurd material—avoid overtly clownish or slapstick approaches when imitating this style; disbelief is the emotional register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clips Juxtaposed to Reveal Contradiction (explicit rubric item)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are clips juxtaposed to reveal contradiction?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly called out in the rubric: editing and clip selection should make contradictions clear rather than merely present them; sequencing matters for the satirical claim.
